Louis XIV and Absolute Monarchy

Louis XIV's Wars and the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes

Mini-lesson · Mr. Magister

A King Against Europe

1Wars for glory: the Dutch flood their land
2One king, one law, one faith
3The Huguenots flee to France's rivals
4The Grand Alliance and the balance of power
5Spain, debts, and a hollow victory
Today's Focus

Did Louis XIV's wars and his war on the Huguenots make France strong, or hollow it out?

Louis XIV wanted glory abroad and one faith at home. Today you will see how his wars frightened Europe into joining against him, how he drove out a talented minority, and what he left behind.

Objectives
  1. Describe the major wars of Louis XIV and how his rivals united against him.
  2. Explain why Louis revoked the Edict of Nantes and what the results were.
  3. Evaluate whether Louis left France stronger or weaker.
Quick Check-in

Louis XIV drove perhaps two hundred thousand Protestants out of France. Before you read: who do you think gained from that?

The Book

Parts 1 to 8

⚡ DECIDE FIRST
It is 1681, and France is at peace. The city of Strasbourg lies on your border, and your lawyers tell you it is rightfully yours. You are Louis XIV, and no one can stop you.
Decide first, and jot your answer in your notebook: would you seize it, and how might your neighbors respond? Then open to compare.
The lesson shows what Louis did: in 1681 he took Strasbourg in peacetime, and his neighbors began to wonder where he would stop. Another path was to press the claim by talks, or to let it drop. [[term:absolute-monarchy|Absolute monarchy]] gave Louis the power to choose without anyone's leave, and the lesson shows that one such choice was followed by others. What a ruler can do and what he should do are different questions, and the cost may fall on other people.
⚡ PUT IT IN ORDER
Tap these events in the order they happened, earliest first.
    ⚡ HOW MUCH WAS HIS DOING?
    The winters of 1693 and 1709 ruined harvests, and the wars made taxes heavier. How much of the suffering of ordinary French people came from the king's own choices?
    The Verdict

    Check What You Learned

    Choose the best answer for each question. The last question asks about the whole lesson.

    Your Answer Now

    The lesson asks whether Louis left France stronger or weaker. Using at least two details from the book, explain why a reader might call his reign strong, and why another might call it hollow.

    Louis XIV's Wars and the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes

    Part 1

    The First Wars

    Chapter 1The First Wars
    Chapter 1

    The First Wars

    Louis wanted glory, and in his day glory meant conquest. Absolute monarchy gave him the power to choose war without asking anyone's leave. His first war, in 1667, was over lands in the Spanish Netherlands, which he claimed through his Spanish wife. England, the Dutch Republic, and Sweden joined together and pushed him to settle the next year, and Louis blamed the Dutch for it. In 1672 he attacked the Dutch Republic with an enormous army. The Dutch called it the Disaster Year. More than a hundred thousand French soldiers marched through town after town, and the Dutch ran out of places to retreat. Louis's terms for peace were so harsh that the Dutch, now led by William, refused them. Their government opened the dikes and flooded the land to stop the French. It ruined farms, but water stopped horses and guns. A mob in The Hague murdered the leaders of the merchant party, the brothers Johan and Cornelis de Witt, who had kept the army small and tried to keep the peace. The young William of Orange, only twenty-one, came to power as stadtholder. He held on. In 1677 he married Mary, the daughter of the English king's brother James. In 1678 the war ended with Louis taking new territory.

    Louis was not satisfied. Even in times of peace, he seized towns on his borders and claimed they were rightfully his. He did it with lawyers before he did it with soldiers. Special French courts studied old treaties and ruled that this town or that district had once depended on land France now held, and troops then arrived to collect. In 1681 he took the city of Strasbourg, a free city of the German empire and the key to the Rhine. French troops surrounded it in September. The city council had no army and no help coming, and it gave in. His neighbors began to wonder where he would stop.

    Louis also looked beyond Europe. Colbert supported colonies in Canada and the Caribbean. In 1682 the explorer La Salle paddled down the Mississippi River and claimed its whole basin for France. He had set out from Canada and reached the Gulf of Mexico in April. He named the region Louisiana in honor of the king. La Salle later tried to plant a colony from the sea, and in 1687 his own men murdered him.

    Part 2

    One King, One Law, One Faith

    Chapter 2One King, One Law, One Faith
    Chapter 2

    One King, One Law, One Faith

    A French saying summed up Louis's goal: one king, one law, one faith. The Huguenots were French Protestants, and there were perhaps a million of them. In 1598 King Henri IV had issued the Edict of Nantes to end the wars of religion, which had torn France apart for more than thirty years. This edict let Huguenots worship in many places and gave them some legal protection.

    Louis believed that a united kingdom needed a single faith, and his bishops agreed. From the 1660s he cut away Huguenot rights. He closed their schools and shut them out of many professions. In 1681 a law allowed children as young as seven to turn Catholic over their parents' wishes. From 1681 his agents used the dragonnade, beginning in the western province of Poitou. They quartered soldiers in Huguenot homes and let them behave as roughly as they liked until the family gave in. Thousands converted to make it stop. Reports reached Versailles that whole districts had turned Catholic, and the numbers looked like a triumph. On October 17, 1685, the Edict of Fontainebleau revoked the Edict of Nantes completely. Protestant churches were to be torn down, pastors were ordered out, and worship was forbidden. Pastors were given two weeks to leave. Ordinary Protestants were forbidden to leave at all, and their children were to be baptized as Catholics. Louis was told that Protestantism in France was finished.

    Part 3

    A Gift to His Rivals

    Chapter 3A Gift to His Rivals
    Chapter 3

    A Gift to His Rivals

    It was not finished. Though the borders were closed to Protestants, perhaps two hundred thousand escaped. They left at night, hid in carts, and walked through forests, because men caught leaving could be sent to row in the galleys. Many were skilled. They included silk weavers, bankers, watchmakers, and army officers. They settled in England, the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, and the German state of Brandenburg-Prussia, whose ruler invited them in the Edict of Potsdam, issued less than two weeks after Louis's edict. In London, silk weavers gathered in the district of Spitalfields. Some sailed to the Dutch colony at the Cape of Good Hope and to North America. Many Huguenot officers went to serve William of Orange. Their descendants include famous Americans. Paul Revere's father, for example, was a Huguenot boy who came to Boston from France and changed his name.

    Louis had meant to strengthen France, but he had armed and enriched his enemies. Protestant Europe was shocked, and it helped to turn opinion against France in the very years William was preparing his invasion of England. Even the king's own engineer, Marshal Vauban, whom you will meet below, wrote to him in 1689 to plead that the Huguenots be allowed to return. He counted the loss in sailors, soldiers, and officers who had gone over to the enemy.

    Part 4

    The King Who Backed the Loser

    Chapter 4The King Who Backed the Loser
    Chapter 4

    The King Who Backed the Loser

    In 1688 William crossed the Channel with a Dutch fleet and army, and James II, abandoned by many of his own officers, fled to France. Louis welcomed him and gave him the palace at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the same palace to which Louis's own mother had once carried him in the night. When William took the English crown in 1689, he was ruling both the Dutch Republic and England, so two sea powers now fought under one command. Louis took the side of the exiled James II. He gave James ships, money, and soldiers to retake Ireland. William defeated them at the Boyne in 1690, and James fled to France once more. Louis had now made himself the enemy of the new English government, and England would be at war with France for most of the next twenty-five years.

    Part 5

    The Grand Alliance

    Chapter 5The Grand Alliance
    Chapter 5

    The Grand Alliance

    In 1688 Louis's attack on the German lands of the Rhine began the Nine Years' War. In 1689 French troops put the Palatinate to the torch, burning towns and blowing up castle walls, so that no enemy army could live off the land. The fires turned German opinion hard against France. This time England, the Dutch Republic, Austria, and others joined together to stop him. The war ended in 1697 with Louis giving up many of his gains, though he kept Strasbourg. This was an early example of the principle of the balance of power. When one state grows strong enough to dominate its neighbors, the others unite against it. Alone, each was weaker than France. Together, they were stronger.

    Part 6

    The Spanish Succession

    Chapter 6The Spanish Succession
    Chapter 6

    The Spanish Succession

    In 1700 the childless king of Spain died. His will left the entire Spanish empire to Louis's grandson, Philip. The dying king, Charles II, had no children, and the powers of Europe had already agreed on a plan to divide his lands, a plan Louis himself had signed. If Philip refused, the will gave everything to an Austrian archduke. Louis's council argued for days. If the French accepted, France and Spain might one day be ruled by one family. Louis accepted anyway, which meant breaking the plan he had signed, and Europe went to war again. When James II died in 1701, Louis also recognized James's son as the rightful king of England. England's rulers took that as an insult.

    In the War of the Spanish Succession, England, the Dutch, and Austria fought France and Spain. The English general Marlborough and the Austrian prince Eugene of Savoy won a famous victory at Blenheim in 1704. Marlborough had marched his army from the Low Countries to the Danube, about 250 miles in five weeks, before the French understood where he was headed. At Blenheim the French commander, Marshal Tallard, was taken prisoner along with more than ten thousand of his men. French armies had seemed unbeatable, and now they were not. Taxes soared, and in the terrible winter of 1709 hunger killed hundreds of thousands.

    In the spring of 1709, with France starving, Louis was ready for peace, and his foreign minister went to the Dutch city of The Hague to ask for terms. The allies' terms were harsh. They demanded that Louis join in forcing his own grandson off the Spanish throne, by French arms if need be. Louis refused. In a letter read aloud in French churches that June, he said that he had sought peace and been refused terms he could not accept, and he asked his people to stand with him. French armies fought on. At Malplaquet that September the allies held the field, but they lost so many men that they could not push farther.

    Then fortune turned. In 1711 the Austrian emperor died, and the throne passed to his brother Charles, the allies' own candidate for Spain. Now the allies faced the prospect that Austria and Spain would be ruled together by one man. Britain had little wish for that, and its leaders began to talk peace. In the Treaties of Utrecht, in 1713 and 1714, Philip kept Spain but his family could never also inherit France. Britain won Gibraltar, Minorca, and Newfoundland, along with the right to sell enslaved Africans in Spain's colonies. Philip stayed on the Spanish throne until 1746. The family he founded, the Spanish Bourbons, still reigns in Spain today.

    Part 7

    The Cost to Ordinary People

    Chapter 7The Cost to Ordinary People
    Chapter 7

    The Cost to Ordinary People

    The burden of war fell heavily on ordinary people. Soldiers had to be fed and clothed, and taxes grew heavier. In 1695 the crown began a head tax, with the rate set by social rank, and in 1710 it tried a tax of a tenth of income. Both were meant to reach the privileged, and both ended up full of exemptions that could be bought. The cold winters of 1693 and 1709 ruined harvests, and many starved. The military engineer Marshal Vauban, who built the great fortresses that guarded France, saw the misery. He had traveled France and seen how people lived, and he proposed a fairer tax on everyone's income, one that nobles and clergy would also pay. Louis rejected the idea and banned the book. Vauban died soon after. His plan went unused, and the problem he named stayed with France for the rest of the century.

    Part 8

    Strong or Hollow?

    Chapter 8Strong or Hollow?
    Chapter 8

    Strong or Hollow?

    Louis died on September 1, 1715, after seventy-two years on the throne. He left a splendid culture and the largest population in Europe. He also left enormous debts. Death had been thinning his family. His son, the Dauphin, died in 1711. In 1712 his grandson, the Duke of Burgundy, died, and within weeks so did Burgundy's wife and their elder son. The heir was now a small child. To his five-year-old great-grandson and heir he is reported to have said, "Do not imitate me in my taste for building, nor in my love of war." Within days of his death, the high court of Paris set aside his will, which had limited the powers of the regent who would rule for the child king.

    So was he strong or hollow? His rule solved the first-order problems of order and defense for many years. But his tax system favored the privileged. His wars drained the treasury, and his religious policy drove skilled people into the arms of his rivals. His successors inherited a government that was proud, rich in show, and short of money. France remained a great power, but the balance had shifted. Britain, with its Parliament, its bank, and its navy, was becoming the leading sea power and the best borrower in Europe. Parliament voted the taxes that paid British debts, and lenders trusted that. A French lender had only the king's word. The struggle between the two would shape the next century, and you will see it in next week's lessons.
